title: Who Is the LORD?
theme: Moses and Aaron bring God's demand to Pharaoh, who scorns the LORD and makes Israel's labor crueler. Obedience to God's word leads first to things getting worse, and Moses brings his bewildered complaint to God.

language.note: 'I do not know the LORD.' Pharaoh's boast sets the agenda for the plagues. From here on God repeatedly says he acts so that Pharaoh, Egypt and Israel 'shall know that I am the LORD' (7:5, 17; 8:10; 14:4).
'Let my people go' uses this verb, which recurs throughout the plague narrative. Pharaoh refuses to 'send' Israel; in the end he will drive them out (12:31-33).
'That they may hold a feast to me in the wilderness.' The goal of the exodus is worship. Israel's later pilgrimage feasts (Passover, Weeks, Booths) use this word.
The foremen see they are 'in trouble' (literally, in evil). Moses asks God why he has 'done evil' to this people. The word can mean moral evil or simply calamity, and here it is calamity.

usage.note: Pharaoh's 'Who is the LORD?' is echoed by Sennacherib and Nebuchadnezzar. Psalm 2 laughs at such kings, and the apostles apply it to those who crucified Jesus.
Moses' 'Why have you done evil to this people?' joins the honest laments of Scripture. Bringing bewilderment to God is itself an act of faith.
Babel built with bricks to make a name; Egypt forces bricks from slaves. Jesus offers a burden that is light.

context.setting: Israel's elders believed and worshiped (4:31). Now Moses and Aaron go to Pharaoh with the request God gave in 3:18. Egyptian records and wall paintings show mud-brick production with straw as a binder, and the quotas and taskmasters described here fit that world.

flow.label: Let my people go
flow.note: Moses and Aaron deliver God's demand; Pharaoh replies that he does not know the LORD and calls the request a distraction from work.

flow.label: Bricks without straw
flow.note: Pharaoh orders that Israel gather their own straw while keeping the same quota. The Hebrew foremen are beaten when the quota is not met.

flow.label: The foremen turn on Moses
flow.note: Pharaoh rejects the foremen's appeal and calls them lazy. They meet Moses and Aaron and blame them for making Israel stink before Pharaoh.

flow.label: Why did you send me?
flow.note: Moses turns to the LORD: you have not delivered your people at all, and since I spoke to Pharaoh he has done evil to them.

tier1.note: God told Moses to ask for a three-day journey and warned that Pharaoh would not let them go unless compelled by a mighty hand.
God answers Moses' complaint immediately with a renewed revelation of his name and seven 'I will' promises.

tier2.note: God's answer to 'I do not know the LORD': the Egyptians shall know that I am the LORD.
Israel's complaint against Moses here begins a pattern that continues through the wilderness.
If they persecuted me, they will persecute you. Following God's call often brings more opposition, not less.

tier3.note: God recalls relieving Israel's shoulder of the burden and freeing their hands from the basket.
Present sufferings are not worth comparing with the glory to be revealed. The darkest point often comes just before deliverance.
Christ set us free so that we would not again submit to a yoke of slavery.

voices.name: Philip Graham Ryken
voices.view: Ryken observes that obeying God made things worse before it made them better, and that this is a normal part of the life of faith. He encourages believers whose obedience brings hardship to bring their questions to God, as Moses did, rather than walk away.

voices.name: Nahum M. Sarna
voices.view: Sarna notes that the brickmaking details fit what is known of Egyptian practice, where straw was mixed into mud bricks and work quotas were recorded. Forcing slaves to gather their own straw multiplied their labor while appearing to change nothing.

translations.kjv: And they said unto them, The LORD look upon you, and judge; because ye have made our savour to be abhorred in the eyes of Pharaoh, and in the eyes of his servants, to put a sword in their hand to slay us.

renderings.text: you have made us stink in the sight of Pharaoh
You have made us obnoxious to Pharaoh

translations.note: The Hebrew is vivid: 'you have made our smell stink.' The same verb is used when the Nile and the frogs stink (7:18; 8:14). Israel feels as offensive to Pharaoh as rotting fish.

steps.gospel: Pharaoh demands more work from slaves who have no strength, and blames them for failing. That is the voice of every false master, including sin and a law kept in our own strength. The gospel announces a Lord who does not add to our burden but carries it, who calls the weary to rest. And like Moses, Jesus came to his people with a word of deliverance and was blamed for their troubles, yet God's rescue went ahead through what looked like defeat.
application: Expect that obedience may bring opposition before it brings relief, and do not take that as proof God has abandoned you.
Bring confusion and disappointment honestly to God in prayer, as Moses did.
Recognize the voice of oppression that says 'work harder, you are lazy.' God's rule is not like Pharaoh's.
Remember that the world's 'Who is the LORD?' will be answered. Every knee will learn who he is.

misapplications.claim: If following God's will makes life harder, you must have misunderstood God's will.
misapplications.correction: Moses did exactly what God said, and God had warned that Pharaoh would refuse (3:19). Hardship after obedience was part of the plan, not a sign of error.

misapplications.claim: Moses sinned by complaining to God.
misapplications.correction: God does not rebuke Moses here; he answers him with promises (6:1-8). Honest lament addressed to God differs from grumbling against him.

contrasts.note: God wants Israel free to hold a feast to him; Pharaoh wants only their labor.
The first move of the exodus seems to fail entirely, setting up God's greater demonstration of power.

contrasts.b: 'You shall know that I am the LORD'
contrasts.note: Pharaoh's question frames the plague narrative; each plague is part of God's answer.

features.label: Two kings' messages
features.note: Verse 1 begins 'Thus says the LORD'; verse 10 begins 'Thus says Pharaoh.' The chapter is a clash of two claims to lordship.

features.label: A chain of blame
features.note: Pharaoh blames Israel, the taskmasters beat the foremen, the foremen blame Moses, and Moses brings it to God. Oppression spreads blame downward.

features.label: Feast versus labor
features.note: Pharaoh calls the request for worship laziness (v8, 17). Rest and worship are a threat to a regime built on endless production.

steps.summary: Exodus 5 sets Pharaoh's claim to lordship against the LORD's. Pharaoh's 'Who is the LORD?' and his crushing response bring Israel lower than before and turn the people against Moses. Yet the darkness makes room for God to show who he is, and Moses rightly brings his complaint to the God who sent him.

metaArc.book: Chapter 5 is the first confrontation with Pharaoh and its apparent failure. It raises the question 'Who is the LORD?' that the plagues answer, and it shows Israel's weakness and tendency to blame, which will mark the wilderness years.
metaArc.redemptive: This belongs to Redemption under strain. Deliverance does not come by negotiation; it will take God's mighty hand, just as human salvation required the decisive act of God in Christ.
